EV02.title: Real A/B registration
EV02.expected_evidence: protected endpoint auth, model profile, distinct physical GPUs and epochs

B.cold_or_warm: Cold for the first launch (no image, no weights, no compile cache); warm for the restart and for the step 3 relaunch, except that changing --max-model-len invalidated the compile cache.
B.sample_count: probe runs: 4 (baseline, post-restart, step 3 origin :8000, step 3 origin :8001); repeated /v1/models calls against one origin: 3; inference smoke requests: 1; runtime restarts: 2
source_observations: SRC-02: the STACK-EVALUATION-PRP section 4 finding that a vLLM api-key alone is not sufficient protection is confirmed here by execution (/metrics served without a credential).
SRC-01: vLLM as candidate B's LLM engine served as the source describes; the identity and registry limitations recorded above are not covered by that source review.
observations: Step 1. The runtime would not start at all under Docker Desktop / WSL2 until VLLM_WSL2_ENABLE_PIN_MEMORY=1 was set: vLLM 0.29.0 disables pinned host memory on WSL2 by default while its V2 GPU model runner requires UVA buffers, so the engine core died with 'UVA is not available'. Root cause and fix in .brain/rca/RCA-2026-09-21-vllm-wsl2-uva.md.

Step 2. No probed endpoint exposed a physical GPU UUID. nvidia-smi on the Windows host matched zero runtime processes because WSL2 GPU paravirtualisation hides them; nvidia-smi inside the container reported GPU-38430611-f42d-0296-a887-d75649b21f25, which equals the UUID already recorded for environment.control_host, and listed the EngineCore pid 131 with process_name '[Not Found]' and used memory '[N/A]'. PRP can therefore join a runtime to a physical GPU only from inside the container, and cannot obtain per-process GPU memory on this substrate.

Step 2. The authenticated model listing exposes no model revision: it returns id, root, max_model_len, owned_by, created and a permission block, so PRP cannot verify from the API that the runtime serves shared_revision ce0a741. The served artifact was instead verified out of band before launch: tokenizer.json sha256 aeb13307a71acd8fe81861d94ad54ab689df773318809eed3cbe794b4492dae4 and chat_template.jinja sha256 64f85b198065d0fba2a81f37e10ed68161ce2c19a754c7100e67e0ca2ee9c326 both match the pinned values, and the two safetensors shards total 8044982000 bytes (7.49 GiB).

Step 2 and step 3, corrected reading. data[0].created and permission[0].id are NOT a restart epoch and NOT runtime identity: three consecutive /v1/models calls against one origin returned three different modelperm-* values, and created tracks the wall clock at request time. The three identifiers that differ in ev02_restart_identity_B_B_20260920T223039Z.json reflect elapsed time between the two snapshots, not the restart.

Step 2. The only stable runtime identity observed is /metrics process_start_time_seconds: identical (1.78994622059e+09) across two origins served by one process, and changed to 1.78994655054e+09 after a deliberate restart. /metrics vllm:cache_config_info also carries the resolved profile (kv_cache_size_tokens, kv_cache_max_concurrency, num_gpu_blocks, gpu_memory_utilization, block_size).

Step 3 case 1, same alias with a different profile. Relaunching the same served-model-name with --max-model-len 4096 instead of 8192 is visible in the listing (max_model_len changes under the same id) and in /metrics. vLLM has no cross-process model registry, so two instances of one alias are never merged or compared by the candidate; distinguishing them is entirely PRP's responsibility.

Step 3 case 2, two origins onto one runtime. With 127.0.0.1:8000 and 127.0.0.1:8001 published to the same container port, the model listing gives a different created and a different permission[0].id per origin, which would lead a consumer that trusts the listing to count one runtime as two capacities. Only /metrics process_start_time_seconds reveals that the two origins are one process.

Step 4. /v1/models returns 401 without a credential but sends no WWW-Authenticate (or equivalent) challenge header. /metrics returns 200 and 52294 bytes of telemetry with no credential at all: --api-key does not cover it, as vLLM's own security documentation states. This confirms the known gap SRC-02 by execution.

Consequence of the previous two observations taken together: the only source of stable runtime identity and of the resolved profile is the one endpoint the candidate's own credential mechanism does not protect. Any PRP design on candidate B must put a network policy or reverse proxy in front of /metrics rather than rely on --api-key.

Operator cost. Weights were mounted from a Windows path through 9P: vLLM logged 'Filesystem type for checkpoints: 9P', disabled auto-prefetch because 9P is not a recognised network filesystem, and took 64.72 s to load the 7.49 GiB checkpoint. Changing --max-model-len invalidated the AOT compile cache and cost 22.13 s of recompilation. Both are properties of running candidate B on Windows, not of vLLM in general.
Inference works end to end: a Thai chat completion returned U+0E01 U+0E23 U+0E38 U+0E07 U+0E40 U+0E17 U+0E1E U+0E2F with finish_reason stop in 254 ms of wall clock.
B.disposition_hint: ADAPT. The candidate reports neither the physical GPU nor a stable runtime identity through its authenticated API; PRP must join the GPU UUID itself from inside the container and must derive node identity and profile from /metrics, which the candidate does not protect. Operator suggestion only; the verdict is the reviewer's.
B.blocker: The two-host portion of step 1 and the cross-host capacity check are unrun because only one GPU host exists in this run window (DEV-03). status and gate_verdicts are left NOT_RUN pending the reviewer's decision.

EV03.title: Target binding
EV03.expected_evidence: request lease matches actual node, including framework routing/retry

B.cold_or_warm: Warm: the vLLM container was restarted from its existing filesystem, so the AOT compile cache for the 4096 profile was reused and the runtime was serving in about 5 s of polling. The LiteLLM proxy had been up since EV04 and was recreated once to pick up the real upstream credential.
B.sample_count: test 1 (live target): 5 requests; test 2 (down target): 5 requests plus 1 manual call to capture the full error body; test 4 (kill mid-generation): 1 request; unauthenticated probe: 2 requests (one per path)
source_observations: SRC-03: the STACK-EVALUATION-PRP section 4 concern that LiteLLM gateway retries could readmit work without PRP knowing is addressed for this configuration — retries and fallbacks are disabled by config and the disabling was confirmed by execution. The absent routing response headers and the HTTP 500 collapsing of distinct upstream failures are not covered by that source review and come from this run.
SRC-02: the vLLM api-key insufficiency recorded at EV02 and EV04 is now confirmed at its strongest form — POST /invocations serves inference with no credential at all.
observations: Test 1, binding. Five requests addressed to wp24-litellm-subspike-host-b all succeeded and vLLM's own access log recorded exactly five POST /v1/chat/completions 200. Five client calls produced five upstream calls, so with num_retries 0 there is no retry amplification and every request landed on the deployment it was addressed to.

Test 1, limitation. No x-litellm-model-id, x-litellm-model-api-base or x-litellm-model-group response header was present on this build, so binding could not be confirmed from the documented response headers and was confirmed by correlating with the upstream engine's access log instead. PRP cannot rely on those headers to learn which node served a request on LiteLLM v1.90.2.

Test 2, no hidden failover. wp24-litellm-subspike-host-a points at port 8010 where nothing listens (connection refused, verified from inside the proxy container) while the live host B runtime stayed healthy. All five requests failed with a client-visible 500 and zero requests reached the live peer. This is the decisive NFR-023 observation obtainable with one GPU: a request bound to a down target is not silently re-routed onto a healthy one.

Test 3, retry and fallback switches confirmed by execution rather than by reading the config: 5 client calls produced 5 upstream calls (no retry), 5 failures produced 0 requests on the peer (no fallback), and the client-visible error states it directly with 'Available Model Group Fallbacks=None'.

Test 3, a counting trap worth recording. The proxy log contains 25 lines matching the word 'fallback', but they are stack-trace frames from litellm/router.py async_function_with_fallbacks — the code path's name, not fallback attempts. Counting the word in logs would have produced the opposite conclusion to the measurements.
Test 3, hedging. No hedging switch exists in the documented surface and no raced duplicate request was observed: the upstream count matched the client count exactly in test 1.

Test 4, kill mid-generation. A 2000-token generation was started against the live host B and the container was killed 4 s in. The client received HTTP 500 after 4.215 s with 'Hosted_vllmException - Server disconnected' and 'Available Model Group Fallbacks=None'. The failure surfaced immediately rather than hanging, and there was no second completion and no replay.

Test 4, caveat recorded rather than glossed. vLLM writes its access-log line when a request completes, so the killed request never produced one. The upstream request count for this test is empty by construction and is not itself evidence of zero upstream requests; the no-replay evidence is the client side.

Cross-cutting, deferred from EV04 by owner decision and now confirmed by request. Straight at the vLLM runtime with no Authorization header, POST /v1/chat/completions returns 401 but POST /invocations returns 200 with a real completion (9 prompt tokens, 2 completion tokens). vLLM's --api-key is bypassable by changing the path, so an unauthenticated caller with network reach to the runtime can consume GPU capacity. A network policy in front of the runtime is mandatory for candidate B, not advisory.

Error shape for the PRP envelope design. Connection refused, a mid-flight disconnect and a genuine internal error all surface as HTTP 500, never 502/503/504, so PRP cannot map LiteLLM status codes onto its own error taxonomy without parsing the message.

Vendor leakage, relevant to NFR-024. The client-visible error body contains the upstream hostname and port (host.docker.internal:8010), the resolved IP (192.168.65.254), the provider class name (Hosted_vllmException) and the internal model-group alias. It must never be forwarded verbatim through the PRP public contract.

Not reachable in this run window, recorded as limits rather than results (DEV-03): no evidence about balancing or shuffling between two healthy deployments, none about mid-flight relocation onto a second live host, and procedure step 4 (a second attempt keeping the original deadline and being readmitted) could not be observed because no second attempt was ever made — which is the correct behaviour for the retry-disabled configuration under test.
B.disposition_hint: CONFIGURE for the binding property itself: with num_retries 0, empty fallback lists, enable_weighted_failover false and disable_cooldowns true, target binding held on every request and nothing was re-routed. Two conditions PRP must carry regardless of the verdict: a network policy in front of the runtime, because POST /invocations bypasses --api-key entirely, and its own error mapping, because every upstream failure arrives as HTTP 500 carrying vendor topology. Operator suggestion only; the verdict is the reviewer's.
B.blocker: Single GPU host (DEV-03): no evidence about two healthy deployments, mid-flight relocation, or procedure step 4's readmitted second attempt. status and gate_verdicts are left NOT_RUN pending the reviewer's decision.

EV04.title: Identity/key semantics
EV04.expected_evidence: hash/verifier or conforming authority, no reveal, scoped listing/jobs/files/revoke

B.cold_or_warm: Cold: the LiteLLM image and postgres:16 were pulled in this run and the proxy started from an empty database. Proxy reached /health/liveliness 200 about 21 s after compose up.
B.sample_count: virtual keys created: 3 (one by ev04_keys.py, two by hand for the storage and isolation checks); readback endpoints probed: 2 (/key/info, /key/list); readback addressing modes: 2 (by plaintext, by sha256 hash); privilege-boundary calls with a virtual key: 4; revoke measurements: 1
B.commands_log: docs/evidence/wp24/WP24-2026-09-20-run1/B/EV04/FINDINGS.md (every command and its result is described there; the raw tool output is in the ev04_*.json artifacts)
source_observations: SRC-03 (LiteLLM as the key/proxy layer of candidate B): the virtual-key mechanism behaves as the source describes for issuance, scoping and revocation. The /key/info cross-key metadata exposure and the plaintext-in-URL log channel are not covered by that source review and come from this run.
SRC-10 (Xinference key recovery) is the FR-005 gap recorded for candidate A and is untouched here: candidate A has not been run.
observations: Bare vLLM, step 1 and 2. vllm/entrypoints/serve/middleware/authenticate.py hashes each configured key with sha256 and compares with secrets.compare_digest, so in process it is a verifier. It is not verifier-only end to end: the plaintext must be supplied through --api-key or VLLM_API_KEY and remains in the process environment, and docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.Env}}' returned the exact key in plaintext (verified by exact-match comparison; the value was never printed).
Bare vLLM, step 2. api_key is a list[str] with no scope of any kind: no organization, application, model, capability, expiry or quota. Revocation means restarting the server; there is no revoke API.

Bare vLLM, step 2. Authentication covers only GUARDED_PREFIX = ('/v1', '/v2', '/inference', '/cohere'). The EV02 route table shows 16 routes outside it, including POST /invocations, POST /tokenize, POST /detokenize, POST /generative_scoring, POST /scale_elastic_ep, POST /is_scaling_elastic_ep, GET /metrics, GET /load, GET /version and the docs routes. vllm/entrypoints/launchers/cli_args.py:290 states this in its own docstring: /invocations 'exposes the same inference capabilities as /v1' and remains unauthenticated. Empirical confirmation that POST /invocations serves inference without a credential is deferred to EV03, which needs the runtime up anyway (owner decision 2026-09-21).

LiteLLM, step 1, correction to the tool's own reading. ev04_keys.py reported plaintext_reappeared_any_channel true and printed an FR-005 FAIL sentence. That is a false positive: line 148 of the script calls GET /key/info?key=<plaintext_key>, so the plaintext in the response is the script's own query parameter echoed back. See .brain/rca/RCA-2026-09-21-ev04-keys-readback-false-positive.md. No FR-005 verdict should be taken from that observation.

LiteLLM, step 1, measured properly. Addressed by sha256 hash, the way a caller who does not hold the key must address it, GET /key/info returns 200 with the plaintext absent from the entire body and $.key holding the hash that was asked with. GET /key/list returns no plaintext. In the database, LiteLLM_VerificationToken.token holds 64 hex characters equal to sha256(plaintext) and key_name holds only a redacted preview. LiteLLM stores and serves virtual keys as hashes.

LiteLLM, step 1, the real disclosure channel. The documented lookup convention GET /key/info?key=<key> places the plaintext key in the URL. Calling it that way once and then searching the proxy container log found the plaintext key in the log exactly once; the same call addressed by hash leaves nothing. This is an integration constraint rather than a storage defect: PRP must address /key/info by hash and keep plaintext out of URLs, or every access log, reverse proxy and log shipper in the path becomes a disclosure channel.

LiteLLM, step 2. Key generation accepted and echoed models, expires, max_budget, tpm_limit, rpm_limit and key_alias, and /key/info additionally exposes team, organization, project and budget fields, so the scope vocabulary FR-006..FR-009 needs exists.

LiteLLM, step 2, privilege boundaries. A virtual key gets 403 on GET /key/list and 401 on POST /key/generate, so it can neither enumerate keys nor mint one. But virtual key A reading GET /key/info?key=<hash of key B> returns 200 with key B's alias, models, expiry, budget and spend. /key/info is not scoped per key: any valid virtual key can read another key's metadata once it knows that key's hash, and LiteLLM documents that hash as the value stored as user_api_key_hash in spend logs. No plaintext is disclosed, but the tenant boundary is not enforced on this route.
LiteLLM, step 3. POST /key/delete returned 200 and the revoked key was already rejected by GET /v1/models on the first poll, 0.000 s later at a 0.2 s polling interval. No grace window was observed.

LiteLLM, step 4. The proxy and its database were brought up from nothing with only a generated master key and a Postgres instance: no Zuri, FUNG or Lalin Studio component and no business database was involved, satisfying what FR-001 asks of first-admin bootstrap.

Clean-up. Both hand-created keys were deleted through POST /key/delete (200 each) and SELECT count(*) FROM LiteLLM_VerificationToken returned 0 afterwards. No key value, master key or database password appears in any committed file.
B.disposition_hint: Split by layer, operator suggestion only. Bare vLLM: BUILD-GAP for FR-003..FR-009 — it has no scope vocabulary, no revoke API and authenticates only four path prefixes. LiteLLM: CONFIGURE for issuance, scoping, storage and revocation, with two conditions PRP must carry itself — address /key/info by hash so no plaintext enters a URL or a log, and do not rely on /key/info for tenant isolation. Whether that is enough to make LiteLLM the key authority, or whether PRP must be its own verifier per ADR (exactly one client-key authority), is the reviewer's call.

EV05.title: Atomic multi-process load
EV05.expected_evidence: no duplicated capacity/quota holds; no bypass direct worker

B.cold_or_warm: Cold: a new container with no compile cache, ready about 220 s after docker run. Both load runs were taken after one warm-up-free start; the at-limit run came first.
B.sample_count: run A (at the limit): 4 requests from 1 process, 39 metric scrapes; run B (3x the limit): 12 requests from 3 processes with distinct PIDs, 82 metric scrapes; every request 256 completion tokens
B.commands_log: docs/evidence/wp24/WP24-2026-09-20-run1/B/EV05/FINDINGS.md, docs/evidence/wp24/WP24-2026-09-20-run1/B/EV05/test-design.md and the command_line field of each ev05_admission_load_B_*.json
source_observations: SRC-02: the vLLM security page's point that endpoint authentication alone is insufficient holds at the network layer too. Publishing on 127.0.0.1 keeps LAN and tailnet callers out, but every process on the GPU host reaches the runtime, and /invocations and /metrics answer without the key.
observations: Step 1: vLLM published on 127.0.0.1:8000 refuses the host's LAN and tailnet addresses from the host and from an unrelated container, but the unrelated container reaches it through host.docker.internal. With /invocations and /metrics answering without the key, the only barrier on this host is not being on this machine; a PRP deployment needs a host-level policy to stop other local processes calling the worker directly.

Step 2: with max_num_seqs 4, twelve concurrent requests from three processes all returned 200 and started in three waves of four. Excess work is queued, not rejected, and never runs beyond the limit: running never exceeded 4 in 121 scrapes.
Step 2: the metrics never over-counted. In no scrape did running plus waiting exceed the client-side upper bound on requests that could have been in the server.

Step 2: one scrape, 0.144 s after release, read 0 running and 0 waiting while all 12 requests had already been sent. The gauges lag intake while requests are parsed and tokenized. That is an under-count, which cannot cause a duplicated capacity hold, but it shows admission cannot rely on the metric alone.

Step 3: max_num_seqs is not exposed by /metrics, /v1/models or /version; only the startup log carries it. /metrics vllm:cache_config_info exposes kv_cache_max_concurrency (1.71 at 8192 tokens), a second ceiling that can be lower than max_num_seqs for long requests.
No bound on the waiting queue was visible and none was probed.
B.disposition_hint: Operator suggestion only. PRP-FR-018: CONFIGURE, with conditions PRP carries itself: set max_num_seqs from PRP's own deployment config (it cannot be read back), treat the running/waiting gauges as a pressure signal that may under-count at burst edges, and account for the KV-cache ceiling on long requests. The bypass part needs a host-level network policy in front of the runtime. PRP-FR-017: no candidate-side blocker observed; the durable admission transaction is PRP's own M4 work.
B.blocker: Step 1b (a probe from a second LAN machine) was deferred by owner decision on 2026-09-22 and the runtime was stopped at 08:14:50Z; it needs the runtime relaunched to run. PRP-FR-017 cannot leave NOT_RUN in WP24: it needs PRP's PostgreSQL admission with fault injection (M4).
